summary: This document describes protocol-independent methods that use a few marking bits in packet headers for performance measurement. The client and server cooperate by marking packets and possibly mirroring marks on the return path. They are especially valuable for protocols that encrypt transport headers, since they still allow loss and delay measurement.

plainLanguage.summary: When the mail is sealed, helpers can't see inside. The sender and receiver agree to put small colored dots on the envelope so everyone can see how fast the mail travels.

questions: how measure delay on encrypted transport
subtitle: Marking bits in packet headers for measuring network delay and loss on encrypted transport.

tldr.problem: Network operators need to measure packet loss and delay on transport protocols that encrypt their headers, like QUIC and TLS over TCP. Traditional measurement methods rely on reading unencrypted sequence numbers and acknowledgments, which are now hidden.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines marking techniques using a few spare bits in the unencrypted portion of transport headers. Endpoints cooperate by toggling these bits in specific patterns, creating measurable signals that on-path observers can detect and analyze without knowing the encrypted content.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now measure latency and loss for encrypted flows passively, enabling better network diagnostics and performance monitoring without requiring changes to application code.

today: RFC 9506 is an Informational RFC published in October 2023. It describes techniques that have been successfully implemented in experimental deployments and provides guidance for transport protocols to incorporate these marking methods. QUIC already includes the Spin bit and has reserved space for other marking bits in its specification.

sections.title: The Problem of Measuring Encrypted Traffic
sections.content:
Network operators need to detect and measure packet loss and delay to maintain good service and fix problems quickly. Traditionally, they monitored the unencrypted fields in TCP headers (sequence and acknowledgment numbers) to measure performance.

With modern encrypted transport protocols like QUIC and TLS-protected TCP, these headers are now encrypted, making passive measurement impossible by the old methods. Since encrypted traffic and unencrypted traffic may be routed differently or behave differently on the network, operators cannot simply measure an unencrypted proxy protocol instead. They need measurements from the actual encrypted flows that users are experiencing.
sections.plainLanguage: When you seal a letter, the post office can't read the address inside anymore. They need the sender and receiver to put special marks on the envelope so they can still see how fast the mail travels.

sections.title: How Marking Bits Work
sections.content:
The RFC proposes adding a small number of dedicated marking bits to the unencrypted portion of transport headers. These bits are not part of the encrypted payload, so intermediate observers can read them. Both endpoints (client and server) must cooperate: they set these bits according to specific algorithms, and observers detect patterns in the marked packets to measure network conditions.

The key insight is that the endpoints deliberately expose just enough information for measurement. Instead of trying to hide the signal, they create a clear, deliberate signal that operators can use. This approach follows RFC 8558, which recommends making path signals explicit rather than trying to infer them from encrypted content.
sections.plainLanguage: Like a driver painting colored dots on the roof in a pattern, the endpoints mark packets in a special way. Observers watch the pattern go by and can tell when packets arrive late or don't arrive at all.

sections.title: Measuring Delay with Latency Bits
sections.content:
The RFC describes two ways to measure round-trip time (RTT). The Spin bit is a simple signal that toggles once per round trip: the client flips it to the opposite value whenever it sees a higher packet number from the server, while the server keeps the same value it receives. This creates a square wave that observers can see, and they measure the time between transitions to calculate RTT.

The Delay bit overcomes limitations of the Spin bit by using a different approach. Only one packet per round trip carries a delay sample marked with the Delay bit set to 1. This packet bounces back and forth between client and server throughout the connection, while both endpoints keep reflecting it in the next packet they send. An observer measures the time between consecutive occurrences of the delay sample to determine RTT with higher accuracy, avoiding the spurious signals that packet reordering can create with the Spin bit.

Observers can also measure partial round-trip times by watching both directions of traffic, allowing them to determine the network delay from client to an observation point versus from that point to the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The Spin bit is like a lighthouse beam that switches on and off each time it makes a full rotation, so watchers can count how many rotations happen between two flashes. The Delay bit is like a special packet that bounces back and forth, and watchers can see exactly how long each bounce takes.

sections.title: Measuring Packet Loss with Loss Bits
sections.content:
The RFC defines five bits for loss measurement, each designed for different scenarios. The T bit (round-trip loss) requires the Spin bit to work: the client marks trains of packets, the server reflects them, and the client reflects again, creating two round trips that observers can compare to measure loss. The Q bit (square bit) is simpler: it alternates between 0 and 1 after every N packets (where N is typically 64), creating a square wave. Observers count how many packets have the same Q value and can detect loss. The L bit (loss event bit) carries a counter: if the transport protocol detects packet loss, it increments an internal counter and marks packets with the L bit set to 1 until the counter reaches zero. Observers count packets with L=1 to measure end-to-end loss.

The R bit (reflection square bit) works alongside the Q bit: it reflects the Q signal in the opposite direction but with variable block sizes based on the actual packets received, enabling better loss measurements. The E bit (ECN-echo event bit) signals congestion information that the receiver reported back to the sender when congestion notification (ECN) is used.

These bits can be used alone or in combinations like Q+L or Q+R to measure loss in different parts of the network path (upstream, downstream, or end-to-end) and to characterize whether loss is random or bursty.
sections.plainLanguage: The loss bits are like different colored markers. One color shows how many cars made it through the entire highway. Another shows if cars got lost between points A and B. By combining markers, watchers can figure out exactly where cars go missing.

sections.title: Implementing and Using the Technique
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that not all marking methods need to be used together. A protocol implementation might use only the Spin bit and Q bit, or perhaps Q and L bits depending on the protocol's capabilities and what measurements the network operator needs. The choice depends on how many spare bits are available in the protocol header and what trade-offs between measurement fidelity and marking overhead are acceptable.

The document describes how these techniques have been successfully implemented in experimental deployments for both QUIC and TCP, tested in data center environments and across the public Internet. Protocols that employ loss detection (like QUIC) can use the L bit directly, while others without per-packet loss detection can use the Q and R bits. The RFC notes that the specific implementation details, such as which bits are actually used for which purpose, should be defined by each transport protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Different protocols can pick which colored markers to use based on what they need to measure. A protocol with lots of spare room might use all the markers. One with tight space constraints might just use the most important ones.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Implications
sections.content:
The marking bits expose network performance information to on-path observers, but this information is not new from a security perspective. Passive loss and delay observations have been part of network operations for decades. Operators already measure these metrics on unencrypted protocols, so the bits do not introduce security vulnerabilities. The L bit signal reveals internal state of the protocol's loss detection machinery, but this can often be inferred by timing packets and observing congestion control responses.

However, the document addresses potential misuse. The Q bit could theoretically help an attacker understand which packets were deliberately skipped for security testing (to detect optimistic ACK attacks in QUIC), but the attacker must first wait to receive an entire block of packets, which limits effectiveness against delay-sensitive applications. Protocols should consider shortening the Q block length when such attacks are a concern.

For privacy, marking bits do not reveal user identity or content, but they do make flows more observable. If these techniques are not widely deployed, endpoints using them might be fingerprinted. Additionally, an observer could theoretically use timing information from delay bits to estimate geolocation, though this is less accurate than other methods. Protocols can add optional delay obfuscation by randomizing the reflection delay on the client side.
sections.plainLanguage: The colored dots tell you about traffic, not about what people are saying. But if everyone doesn't use them, someone might be able to tell apart the protocol from dots alone. And if someone knows your exact RTT, they might guess where you're calling from.

fields.name: Spin bit
fields.desc: Toggles once per round trip to create a square wave that observers can measure.

fields.name: Q bit
fields.desc: Toggles after every N packets to mark blocks for upstream loss measurement.

fields.name: R bit
fields.desc: Reflects the Q signal in the opposite direction with variable block sizes.

fields.name: L bit
fields.desc: Set when the sender has unreported losses to signal end-to-end loss.

fields.name: E bit
fields.desc: Set when ECN congestion is reported by the receiver.
